notes.definition: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies produced from a single clone of cells. They are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen, so they can target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.
explanation: Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). Each antibody has a shape that is complementary to one particular antigen, so it binds only to that antigen. 'Monoclonal' means 'from one clone': monoclonal antibodies are all made by a single clone of genetically identical cells, so every antibody is identical. They are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen, which means they can be used to target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.

There is a problem in making large amounts of one antibody. Lymphocytes make antibodies but they do not divide in culture, so only a small amount of antibody can be obtained from them. Tumour (cancer) cells divide rapidly and keep dividing, but they do not make antibodies. The solution is to combine the two types of cell.

Production starts by stimulating mouse lymphocytes to make a particular antibody. A mouse is injected with the chosen antigen. The mouse's lymphocytes respond by producing antibodies specific to that antigen. These lymphocytes are then collected from the mouse.

The lymphocytes are combined (fused) with a particular kind of tumour cell to make a cell called a hybridoma cell. A hybridoma cell has useful features of both parent cells: it can make the specific antibody (from the lymphocyte) and it can divide (from the tumour cell).

Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells. Because they all come from one hybridoma cell, every cell in the clone makes exactly the same antibody. The cells are grown in large quantities, and a large amount of the antibody can be collected from them and purified so it can be used in tests and treatments.
keyFacts: Monoclonal antibodies are produced from a single clone of cells.
They are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen.
This means they can target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.
Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated (by injecting an antigen) to make a particular antibody.
Lymphocytes make antibodies but do not divide; tumour cells divide but do not make antibodies.
A lymphocyte is combined with a tumour cell to make a hybridoma cell.
A hybridoma cell can both divide and make the antibody.
Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all make the same antibody.
A large amount of the antibody can be collected and purified.

keyTerms.definition: A protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
A molecule, usually a protein on the surface of a cell or pathogen, that an antibody binds to.
A type of white blood cell that produces antibodies.
One of many identical antibodies produced from a single clone of cells, specific to one binding site on one protein antigen.
A cell made by combining a lymphocyte with a tumour cell, which can both divide and make a particular antibody.
A group of genetically identical cells produced from one original cell.
A cancer cell that divides rapidly and continuously.

workedExamples.title: Explaining why a hybridoma is needed
workedExamples.question: Explain why scientists fuse lymphocytes with tumour cells to produce monoclonal antibodies.
steps: Lymphocytes can make the specific antibody, but they do not divide in culture, so only small amounts can be made.
Tumour cells divide rapidly, but they do not make the antibody.
Fusing them makes a hybridoma cell, which has both properties.
The hybridoma can be cloned to give many cells that all make the same antibody, so large amounts can be collected.
workedExamples.answer: The hybridoma cell can both make the antibody (from the lymphocyte) and divide (from the tumour cell), so large amounts of one antibody can be produced.

workedExamples.title: Putting the steps in order
workedExamples.question: Put these steps in order: A clone the hybridoma cells; B inject a mouse with the antigen; C collect and purify the antibody; D fuse lymphocytes with tumour cells; E collect lymphocytes that make the antibody.
steps: First the mouse must be stimulated to make the antibody: B.
Then the lymphocytes making the antibody are collected: E.
They are fused with tumour cells to make hybridomas: D.
A single hybridoma cell is cloned: A.
Finally the antibody is collected and purified: C.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think monoclonal antibodies are made by human lymphocytes taken from patients.
misconceptions.right: In fact the specification describes stimulating mouse lymphocytes to make the antibody.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the tumour cell makes the antibody.
misconceptions.right: In fact the tumour cell provides the ability to divide. The lymphocyte provides the ability to make the specific antibody. The hybridoma does both.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 'monoclonal' means the antibody can bind to many different antigens.
misconceptions.right: In fact monoclonal antibodies are all identical and are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think lymphocytes alone can be grown to make large amounts of antibody.
misconceptions.right: In fact lymphocytes do not divide in culture, which is why they must be fused with tumour cells.

realWorld: Monoclonal antibodies made this way are used in pregnancy test sticks to detect the hormone hCG in urine.
Many modern cancer treatments, such as trastuzumab (Herceptin) for some breast cancers, are monoclonal antibodies.
The hybridoma technique was developed in 1975 by Georges Köhler and César Milstein, who received a Nobel Prize for it.
higherTier: This whole subtopic is Higher tier only: how monoclonal antibodies are produced using mouse lymphocytes, tumour cells and hybridoma cells.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology only (not Combined Science Trilogy): monoclonal antibodies are produced from a single clone of hybridoma cells, made by combining mouse lymphocytes with tumour cells.
examTips: Learn the sequence: stimulate mouse lymphocytes → combine with tumour cell → hybridoma → clone single hybridoma → collect and purify antibody.
Say exactly what each parent cell contributes: lymphocyte = makes the antibody; tumour cell = divides.
Use the word 'specific' and the phrase 'one binding site on one protein antigen' when describing monoclonal antibodies.
Use 'combined' or 'fused' for joining the cells, and 'cloned' for producing many identical hybridoma cells.
Do not confuse this subtopic with vaccination: here the mouse is used to produce an antibody for us to collect, not to make the mouse immune.
summary: Monoclonal antibodies come from a single clone of cells and are all identical.
They bind to one binding site on one protein antigen, so they target specific chemicals or cells.
Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make the antibody.
Lymphocytes are combined with tumour cells to make hybridoma cells.
Hybridoma cells can divide and make the antibody.
A single hybridoma is cloned, and the antibody is collected and purified.

questions.question: Which type of cell produces antibodies?
options: Red blood cell
Lymphocyte
Phagocyte
Platelet
markScheme: 1 mark: Lymphocyte
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes make antibodies. Phagocytes engulf pathogens, red blood cells carry oxygen and platelets help clotting.

questions.question: What is a hybridoma cell?
options: A tumour cell that makes antibodies naturally
A lymphocyte that has been cloned
A cell made by combining a lymphocyte and a tumour cell
A mouse cell infected with a virus
markScheme: 1 mark: A cell made by combining a lymphocyte and a tumour cell
questions.explanation: A hybridoma is the result of fusing a lymphocyte with a tumour cell.

questions.question: Which animal's lymphocytes are stimulated to make the antibody?
options: Rabbit
Human
Sheep
Mouse
markScheme: 1 mark: Mouse
questions.explanation: The specification describes stimulating mouse lymphocytes to make a particular antibody.

questions.question: What does the word 'monoclonal' tell you about the antibodies?
options: They are all produced from a single clone of cells
They bind to many different antigens
They are produced by one mouse only
They can only be used once
markScheme: 1 mark: They are all produced from a single clone of cells
questions.explanation: 'Mono' means one and 'clonal' means from a clone: the antibodies all come from one clone of identical cells, so they are identical.

questions.question: Which property does the tumour cell contribute to the hybridoma cell?
options: The ability to make a specific antibody
The ability to divide
The ability to engulf pathogens
The ability to recognise antigens
markScheme: 1 mark: The ability to divide
questions.explanation: Tumour cells divide rapidly. The ability to make the specific antibody comes from the lymphocyte.

questions.question: Why are monoclonal antibodies able to target specific cells in the body?
options: They are very small
They contain a tumour cell
They are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen
They are made by mice
markScheme: 1 mark: They are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen
questions.explanation: Each monoclonal antibody binds only to its specific antigen, so it attaches only to cells or chemicals carrying that antigen.

questions.question: What is the first step in producing a monoclonal antibody?
options: Cloning hybridoma cells
Purifying the antibody
Combining lymphocytes with tumour cells
Stimulating mouse lymphocytes to make the antibody
markScheme: 1 mark: Stimulating mouse lymphocytes to make the antibody
questions.explanation: The mouse is first injected with the antigen so its lymphocytes make the particular antibody. Only then can they be fused with tumour cells.

questions.question: Why are single hybridoma cells cloned?
options: To produce many identical cells that all make the same antibody
To make cells that produce many different antibodies
To stop the cells dividing
To remove the tumour cell properties
markScheme: 1 mark: To produce many identical cells that all make the same antibody
questions.explanation: Cloning one hybridoma cell gives a population of genetically identical cells, so all the antibody produced is identical.

questions.question: A scientist fuses lymphocytes from a mouse injected with antigen X with tumour cells, but grows ALL the hybridomas together without cloning single cells. What is the most likely result?
options: Identical antibodies against antigen X only
No antibodies, because the cells cannot divide
A mixture of different antibodies, not all identical
Antibodies produced by the tumour cells only
markScheme: 1 mark: A mixture of different antibodies, not all identical
questions.explanation: Different lymphocytes make different antibodies, so a mixed culture of hybridomas would produce a mixture. Cloning a single hybridoma gives identical (monoclonal) antibodies.

questions.question: Which row correctly describes the cells used to make monoclonal antibodies?
options: Lymphocyte: divides, makes antibody; tumour cell: divides only
Lymphocyte: makes antibody, does not divide; tumour cell: divides, no antibody
Lymphocyte: divides, no antibody; tumour cell: makes antibody, does not divide
Lymphocyte and tumour cell: both make antibody
markScheme: 1 mark: Lymphocyte: makes antibody, does not divide; tumour cell: divides, no antibody
questions.explanation: Each parent cell has only one of the needed properties, which is why they are combined into a hybridoma.

questions.question: Name the cell formed when a lymphocyte is combined with a tumour cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: hybridoma (cell)
questions.explanation: The fused cell is called a hybridoma cell.

questions.question: State the two things a hybridoma cell can do.
markScheme: 1 mark: divide
1 mark: make/produce the (specific) antibody
questions.explanation: A hybridoma combines the ability to divide (tumour cell) and to make a specific antibody (lymphocyte).

questions.question: State what is done to the antibody after it has been collected from the hybridoma cells.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is purified
questions.explanation: The antibody is collected and purified so it can be used safely in tests or treatments.

questions.question: What type of biological molecule is an antibody?
markScheme: 1 mark: protein
questions.explanation: Antibodies are proteins, which is why each can have a specific shape that binds one antigen.

questions.question: Explain how a mouse is made to produce lymphocytes that make a particular antibody.
markScheme: 1 mark: the mouse is injected with the (specific) antigen
1 mark: its lymphocytes are stimulated to produce antibodies specific to that antigen
questions.explanation: The immune response of the mouse to the injected antigen stimulates lymphocytes to make the complementary antibody.

questions.question: Explain why lymphocytes are combined with tumour cells, rather than being grown on their own, to make large amounts of antibody.
markScheme: 1 mark: lymphocytes do not divide (so cannot be grown in large numbers)
1 mark: tumour cells divide rapidly, so the hybridoma can divide and make the antibody
questions.explanation: Combining the cells gives the hybridoma the ability to multiply while still making the antibody.

questions.question: Explain why all the antibodies produced from one clone of hybridoma cells are identical.
markScheme: 1 mark: the clone comes from a single hybridoma cell
1 mark: so all the cells are genetically identical and make the same antibody
questions.explanation: A clone is a group of genetically identical cells from one parent cell, so they produce identical antibodies.

questions.question: Monoclonal antibodies are described as 'specific'. Explain what this means.
markScheme: 1 mark: they bind to one binding site on one (protein) antigen
1 mark: so they only bind to/target one specific chemical or cell type
questions.explanation: The antibody's shape is complementary to only one antigen, so it attaches to that and nothing else.

questions.question: Suggest why a scientist must test the cloned hybridoma cells to check which antibody they produce before growing them in large quantities.
acceptedAnswers: only some make the wanted antibody
markScheme: 1 mark: the mouse has many lymphocytes making different antibodies
1 mark: so different hybridomas make different antibodies / some will not make the wanted antibody
1 mark: testing selects the clone that makes the antibody specific to the chosen antigen
questions.explanation: Not every lymphocyte collected from the mouse makes the antibody for the injected antigen, so only the right clone should be grown.

questions.question: Monoclonal antibodies made using mouse lymphocytes can sometimes cause an immune response when given to humans. Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the antibodies are mouse proteins, so they are foreign to the human body
1 mark: so the human immune system recognises them as antigens and makes antibodies against them
questions.explanation: Antibodies are proteins. Proteins from another species can be recognised as foreign, which is one reason monoclonal antibodies have caused more side effects than expected.

questions.question: Explain why tumour cells, rather than another type of body cell, are used to produce hybridomas.
markScheme: 1 mark: tumour cells divide rapidly / continuously (uncontrolled)
1 mark: so a very large number of antibody-producing cells (and a large amount of antibody) can be made
questions.explanation: Normal body cells stop dividing after a number of divisions; tumour cells keep dividing, so the hybridoma clone can be grown indefinitely.

questions.question: Suggest one ethical objection some people have to the way monoclonal antibodies are produced, and give one argument in favour.
markScheme: 1 mark: objection, e.g. mice are injected and used / animal welfare concerns
1 mark: argument for, e.g. the antibodies are used to diagnose or treat diseases and save human lives
questions.explanation: The use of animals raises welfare concerns, but the benefits for medicine are considerable. Either side needs a reason.

questions.question: Name the process used to produce many identical hybridoma cells from one hybridoma cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: cloning (accept cell division by mitosis)
questions.explanation: Single hybridoma cells are cloned; the cells divide by mitosis to give genetically identical cells.

questions.question: Describe the roles of the lymphocyte and the tumour cell in producing monoclonal antibodies.
markScheme: Indicative content: lymphocytes make antibodies; mouse lymphocytes stimulated by antigen make a particular antibody; lymphocytes do not divide; tumour cells divide rapidly/continuously; tumour cells do not make antibody; the two are combined to form a hybridoma; hybridoma can divide and make the antibody.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of what each cell contributes and how they are combined into a hybridoma.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statement about one or both cells.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key is to match each cell to the property it provides and explain why both are needed together.

questions.question: Explain how monoclonal antibodies are produced.
markScheme: Indicative content: a mouse is injected with a specific antigen; mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make a particular antibody; lymphocytes are collected; lymphocytes make antibody but do not divide; lymphocytes are combined/fused with a tumour cell; tumour cells divide rapidly; this makes a hybridoma cell; the hybridoma can both divide and make the antibody; a single hybridoma cell is selected and cloned; producing many identical cells that all make the same antibody; antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen; a large amount of the antibody is collected and purified.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, logically sequenced explanation including why lymphocytes are fused with tumour cells and why single hybridomas are cloned.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most stages described in a reasonable order with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. lymphocytes and tumour cells are joined.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both the sequence and the reasons: why the mouse is injected, why fuse with a tumour cell, why clone a single hybridoma.

questions.question: A company needs a large amount of an antibody that binds only to a protein found on the surface of one type of cancer cell. Explain why monoclonal antibody technology is suitable for this, and outline how the antibody would be made.
markScheme: Indicative content: monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen; so would bind only to the cancer cell protein and not to other cells; inject mouse with the cancer cell protein; lymphocytes make antibody; fuse with tumour cells to form hybridomas; clone single hybridoma; hybridomas divide so large amounts can be made; collect and purify.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): links specificity to the target and outlines production including hybridoma formation and cloning to give large amounts.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about specificity or production.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Two ideas are needed: specificity (why it suits the job) and the hybridoma method (how large amounts are made).
